newsitem.title: TURKMENISTAN: Proud Turkmen chief has big plans for desert land.
newsitem.headline: Proud Turkmen chief has big plans for desert land.

text.p: Turkmen President Saparmurat Niyazov, "Turkmenbashi" or leader of the Turkmens, has used a regional summit to impress the neighbours with grand plans for this sleepy desert republic.
The quiet streets of the capital Ashgabat were swept clean for Tuesday's summit, called to work out ways of opening up resource-rich but landlocked Central Asia to world markets.

But Iranian, Turkish and other leaders who attended can hardly have failed to notice Niyazov's five-year-old personality cult, which of late has taken on the tones of a surreal film by Italian director Federico Fellini.
Neon signs dotted around the city flash at night: "People, Motherland, Turkmenbashi!"
The official press has announced plans to build a 70-metre (yards) tower next to the presidential palace with a 12-metre (yards) revolving statue of Niyazov placed on top.
A giant hoarding of Niyazov -- a suit and tie in place of Stalinist khaki tunics -- served as the backdrop for an honour guard which wilted in the heat in front of the president's brand new palace.
The vast building of gleaming white marble, topped with a golden dome, towers above the low-rise city -- flattened in an earthquake in 1947 -- in keeping with Niyazov's political ambitions.
Water gushes down its steps in an elaborate fountain in front of the French-built palace -- most homes in the capital are rationed to only 2-3 hours of water a day.
"All these new fountains mean we lose our water pressure," said one disgruntled resident.

Ashgabat, tucked between the purple Kopet Dagh mountains and the harsh Kara Kum, or "Black Sands", desert, was a Russian colonial backwater built in the 19th century to reinforce Tsarist gains in Central Asia.

One J.T. Woolrych-Perowne, a Briton who went on the first ever Cook's Tour of the region at the turn of the century, said of Ashgabat: "Those of us who had been in India at once saw the resemblance of the place to an ordinary Indian cantonment."
Bored Russian officers gave the tourist and supposed English foe a bear-hug of a welcome, putting on mock cavalry charges against Turkmen horsemen and uncorking the champagne.

The champagne -- and Soviet vodka -- has been replaced by a rum-based cocktail called "desert breeze" in Ashgabat's new rash of largely empty luxury hotels, more in line with Niyazov's grandiose plans for the republic of 3.8 million.

He envisages energy-rich Turkmenistan as a bustling hub, with railways and oil pipelines to replace the camels which once plodded the silk route at the peril of wild Turkmen raiders on the look out for slaves and booty.

The Turkmen leader also wants the neutral republic to be a power of consequence in the region. "Ashgabat could become a Central Asian Geneva," he said recently. "It is not necessary to go a long way to sit at a negotiating table."
This might help fill the hotels. But the region's wars and political bickering and not much cash floating around sees Niyazov a long way from creating his Caspian Kuwait.
